title: How do you handle exceptions globally in Spring Boot REST API using @ControllerAdvice/@RestControllerAdvice, @ExceptionHandler, @ResponseStatus, and ResponseStatusException?
keyPoints: @RestControllerAdvice is a global exception handler class that catches exceptions from all controllers in the application
@ExceptionHandler(XException.class) methods catch specific exception types and return structured error responses with HTTP status codes
Controllers have ZERO try-catch blocks because all exceptions propagate to the global handler automatically
ResponseStatusException (Spring 5) allows inline exception throwing with HTTP status: throw new ResponseStatusException(NOT_FOUND)
Order handlers from most specific to least specific, with a catch-all Exception handler returning 500 for unexpected errors
Never expose internal details like SQL errors or stack traces to the API client in error responses

s1_definition.oneliner: @RestControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler methods provides centralized exception handling for all controllers, returning consistent structured error responses with appropriate HTTP status codes.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **`@RestControllerAdvice`** (or `@ControllerAdvice`) is a class-level annotation that acts as a global exception handler for all controllers in the application.
- **`@ExceptionHandler(XException.class)`** on a method catches a specific exception type thrown by any controller and returns a structured error response.
- **`@ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)`** on the handler method sets the HTTP status code.
- **`ResponseStatusException`** (Spring 5) is an inline alternative: `throw new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "Trade not found")`.
- The result: controllers have **zero try-catch** blocks. All exceptions propagate to the global handler, which returns consistent error responses across the entire API.
s1_definition.analogy: Instead of every teller at National Bank of India having their own error procedure, the bank has a central complaints desk (@ControllerAdvice). Any complaint from any counter goes to this desk. The desk handles each type: insufficient funds returns 400, trade not found returns 404, and system error returns 500. Tellers just do their job without worrying about error handling.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Request
    │
    ▼
  Controller.settle(id)
    │
    │  exception thrown
    ▼
  @RestControllerAdvice
  GlobalExceptionHandler
    │
    ├── TradeNotFoundException     ──▶  404 + ErrorResponse
    ├── InsufficientBalance        ──▶  400 + ErrorResponse
    ├── IllegalArgumentException   ──▶  400 + ErrorResponse
    ├── MethodArgumentNotValid     ──▶  422 + ErrorResponse
    └── Exception (catch-all)      ──▶  500 + ErrorResponse
    │
    ▼
  JSON Response to Client
  {
    "error": "NOT_FOUND",
    "message": "Trade TRD-001 not found",
    "status": 404,
    "timestamp": "2024-01-15T10:30:00Z"
  }
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
@RestControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler methods is the Spring Boot standard for global exception handling. Each handler catches a specific exception type from any controller and returns a structured ErrorResponse with the correct HTTP status. Controllers have zero try-catch blocks. They call the service, and any exception propagates automatically to the global handler.

At National Bank of India, Pankaj's API uses one GlobalExceptionHandler class that maps TradeNotFoundException to 404, InsufficientBalanceException to 400, IllegalArgumentException to 400, and the catch-all Exception to 500. Before this pattern, there were 200 try-catch blocks across 15 controllers with inconsistent error formats. After: one handler class, consistent JSON responses, and controllers focused purely on business logic.

Best practices: order handlers from most specific to least specific. Log the full stack trace in the catch-all handler with `log.error("msg", e)`. Never expose SQL errors, class names, or stack traces to the API client. Include a correlation ID in the error response for distributed tracing.

Remember one sentence: @RestControllerAdvice centralizes exception handling so controllers have zero try-catch and every error returns a consistent structured response.
